name: Iban
confidence_why: Asmah Haji Omar's grammar (1969/1981, pp. 69-70) gives final stress, but only as a non-phonemic intonation element tied to emphasis, and Scott (1957: 509) reports just 'slightly increased stress on the final syllable' for words in isolation, whereas Richards's standard dictionary (1981: xiv-xv) states an explicit word-level penultimate-unless-schwa rule, stable under affixation and with worked examples, which Adelaar (1992: 23), the leading Malayic comparativist, adopts with Asmah and Scott in hand, and Howell & Bailey (1900: viii) also accent the first syllable of disyllables; the remaining final-stress witness, Anonby (2020), describes Sebuyau rather than Iban proper in a non-phonological dissertation, so two authoritative first-hand accounts disagree on the placement of main stress and no third source settles it.
catalog_quote: intonation is regarded as comprising stress, pitch and vowel quantity. These three elements are not phonemic. ... Stress in Iban always falls on the final syllable of a word. Any word receiving emphasis, with or without an emphasizing word (cf. 4.37), is stressed.

new_statements.quote: The usual Sebuyau word is disyllabic, with ultimate stress. These new forms using uwa are trisyllabic with penultimate stress. This is unusual, as very few words have penultimate stress in Malayic and Ibanic. (p. 126) [...] As explained above, most Iban words are disyllabic, with stress on the final syllable. (p. 131) [...] The stress is on the final syllable of Malay and Ibanic disyllabic words. (p. 134) [...] Sebuyau tokens in my texts also usually stress the ultimate syllable. English nouns usually do not. [...] So 'button' [ˈbʌt(ə)n] (which has penultimate stress) when borrowed by the Sebuyau, becomes batan [bʌˈtʌn], with stress on the last vowel. (p. 191)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records Iban as penultimate; Anonby states ultimate (final) stress for Sebuyau and asserts the same for Iban and Ibanic generally, and says penultimate stress is rare. Placement differs outright. His evidence is his own recorded texts from 24 Sebuyau speakers in Lundu District; the Iban-proper claim is unsupported by citation and runs against Richards 1981 and Adelaar 1992 (below). Note the schwa-penult words he cites (empa', enggau, endur) would be final-stressed under the Richards/Adelaar rule too, so part of the disagreement may be about which syllable types dominate the lexicon, but bangku [bãŋˈku] and batan [bʌˈtʌn] (non-schwa penult, final stress) are a real c…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Sebuyau (which Anonby concludes is a variety of Iban) word stress is on the final syllable of the normal disyllabic word; loanwords are re-stressed to the final syllable (batan, bangku [bãŋˈku], derebo [dərəˈbo]). The only penultimate-stressed native forms he notes are the trisyllabic -uwa- forms (Malay final u > Ibanic uwa), which he calls unusual because 'very few words have penultimate stress in Malayic and Ibanic'. He extends the final-stress claim to Iban proper (p. 131, p. 134) without citing a source for it.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic uwa-forms (about 4% of words in his texts) carry penultimate stress; monosyllables (69% of unmodified loans) fall outside the rule. Notes that the Iban/Sebuyau initial schwa before a nasal is 'unstressed' and often dropped in Sebuyau (nggau for enggau, p. 131). Observes Clynes & Deterding (2011) found no inherent lexical stress in Peninsular Malay and Don et al. (2008) found it usually penultimate, whereas his Borneo Malay and Sebuyau data are 'almost always' ultimate.
new_statements.identity_note: Anonby 2020 describes Sebuyau, spoken around Lundu (south-west Sarawak) and studied through 24 speakers of the Keluarga Church community; he concludes (with Anderbeck 2018 and Steinmayer 1999/2012) that it is a variety of Iban, though no longer fully mutually intelligible with Iban proper. Richards 1981 records standard Iban of Sarawak (his dictionary work centred on the Saribas/Second Division; he notes Saribas, Lemanak, Ulu Ai and Upper Rejang variants on p. xiv). Adelaar 1992's IBN data come from Scott's 1956 Sea Dayak dictionary and Richards 1981, i.e. the same standard Iban.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Iban stress is penultimate, except that a penultimate schwa cannot carry it, in which case stress falls on the final syllable; stress is non-phonemic and there are no other contrastive suprasegmentals. new_statements.quote: No stress marks have been used in the dictionary because the general rule is that [stress falls on the pe]nultimate syllable, unless the vowel is e. new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate) with the schwa exception and its sub-exceptions spelled out; stress is stable under affixation and nasal substitution. Richards' dictionary reflects standard (largely Saribas/Second Division) Iban.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on the penultimate syllable unless that syllable's vowel is e (schwa), in which case it goes to the final syllable (te-BANG, le-MAM-bang, nge-MA'); nasal substitution and affixation do not change the rule (stress stays on the penult of the derived word: TI-bang, be-TI-bang; te-BANG, pe-ne-BANG). Bold-type examples on p. xv mark the stressed syllable. The bottom line of p. xiv is partly cropped in the scan; the bracketed words are the legible remains, the rest is verbatim from the page scan.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; in the exception cases (schwa penult closed by a nasal, final closed syllable) stress is said to fall 'evenly on the penultimate and the final' (level stress).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) orthographic e written after r but not pronounced (ter-e-bai = TER-bai 'fly', ker-e-ja = KER-ja 'work'); (b) penultimate e closed by a nasal before a consonant, incl. initial em-/en-/eng- (EM-pa' 'eat', EN-tah, ENG-gai) and CVN-CVC words (REN-tap, TEN-tang, BEM-ban, TEM-pit): these keep the stress on the e-penult. Stress is 'greatly varied' in the recital of pengap invocations. Also p. xiv 'Spelling': the epenthetic e 'should never be allowed to lengthen or carry stress'; where a written e does carry stress Richards spells it i (perintah).

tone_statements.summary: Penultimate default with schwa-conditioned final stress (Richards 1981 adds a cluster exception that keeps stress on a schwa penult before r+C or homorganic NC) versus the catalog's fixed final rule (Asmah Haji Omar 1969). IBN description rests on Scott 1956 (primary lexical source) and Richards 1981, not the author's own data. Confirms no-tone.

readall_conflicts: Richards (1981: xiv-xv) and Adelaar (1992: 23, following Scott 1956 and Richards) agree: Iban stress is penultimate, non-phonemic, and shifts to the final syllable only when the penult has schwa (with Richards' sub-exceptions where a nasal-closed or orthographic-only schwa penult keeps it). Anonby (2020: 126, 131, 134, 191) contradicts this: for Sebuyau (Lundu District), which he treats as a variety of Iban, he reports ultimate stress on the normal disyllable, re-stressing of loans to the final syllable even with a non-schwa penult (bangku [bãŋˈku], batan [bʌˈtʌn]), and calls penultimate stress rare in Malayic and Ibanic generally; he extends the final-stress claim to Iban proper without a citation. The disagreement is partly dialectal (Sebuyau vs. standard/Saribas Iban), partly methodological (Anonby's impressionistic transcription of loanword tokens vs. Richards' lexicographic rule), and Anonby himself notes the same ultimate-vs-penultimate disagreement in the Malay literature (Clynes & Deterding 2011 no lexical stress; Don et al. 2008 penultimate). The catalog's penultimate reading stands for Iban proper; Anonby's final-stress statement should be logged as a dialect-specific (Sebuyau) contradiction, not a reclassify.
